To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Soviet Union failed to develop a steam-turbine aircraft engine because its R&D system was not capable of solving a difficult technical problem.

the Soviet economy failed to produce an efficient allocation of resources, and the reason is that the agents of the economy were not subject to the incentives and constraints that are required for efficiency to prevail.
Soviet R&D failure was the outcome of a principal-agent interaction that was not fully successful.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between politics and economics.
the political economy of R&D failure in the interwar USSR.

the interaction of political and economic forces, with the role of information and incentives in a command economy, and with the role of R&D failure and sunk costs in a system of periodic budget constraints.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Soviet system failed to allocate resources efficiently to R&D projects.
the Soviet R&D system failed to deliver the desired results.
this case of R&D failure was the result of a complex interplay of factors, some of them specific to the interwar Soviet context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

R&D agents did not have sufficient incentive or information to make rational decisions about the allocation of scarce funds, and principals did not have the information needed to make informed choices.
the Soviet system of R&D funding was inefficient, but that it was not the main cause of R&D failures.
the Soviet economy was not a command economy in the sense of being run by a central planner, but that the system was not a market economy either.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Soviet system was a poor one for the evaluation of R&D projects.
the Soviet system was not designed for R&D success.
Soviet military R&D was a complex process that cannot be explained by any single theory.
